subject: Banking
title: Crypto as a Payment System
description: A 60-second lesson on Crypto as a Payment System.

hook.text: Bitcoin was designed to replace banks for payments. But 15 years later, people mostly hold it instead of spending it.

buildup.text: Bitcoin transactions take 10-60 minutes to confirm and cost $1-30 in fees depending on network congestion.

discovery.text: Layer-2 solutions like Lightning Network make Bitcoin payments nearly instant and almost free. The tech is improving.

twist.text: People hesitate to spend an asset that might jump 10% tomorrow, so a currency becomes a collectible.

climax.text: Crypto works for transfers and speculation. As everyday payment, volatility and speed remain real obstacles.

punchline.text: Designed for payments, used for holding. Crypto's payment promise waits.

quiz.question: Why hasn't Bitcoin become a widely used payment method?
options: Price volatility and slow confirmation times make daily payments impractical

details.summary: Cryptocurrencies were designed as peer-to-peer payment systems that bypass banks entirely, but slow transaction speeds, volatile prices, and high fees have limited their use as everyday payment methods.
details.whyItMatters: Despite the hype, crypto has failed to become a practical payment system for daily use. Understanding why reveals the gap between decentralized ideals and the practical requirements of functional payments.
takeaways: Bitcoin processes roughly 7 transactions per second versus Visa's 65,000
Price volatility makes crypto impractical for pricing goods and services
Lightning Network and Layer 2 solutions attempt to solve speed issues

faq.question: Why did Bitcoin fail as a payment system?
faq.answer: Transaction fees spike during high demand, confirmation takes 10 minutes minimum, and price volatility means the value changes between sending and receiving. These make it unsuitable for buying everyday goods.

faq.question: Are stablecoins better for payments than Bitcoin?
faq.answer: Yes, for stability. Stablecoins like USDC maintain a fixed value pegged to the dollar, solving the volatility problem. But they still face speed, cost, and regulatory challenges that limit mainstream payment adoption.
